title: Informal ECOFIN Opens in Nicosia — Finance Ministers and ECB Governors Discuss Stablecoins and Competitiveness
detail: EU Finance Ministers and European Central Bank Governors gathered in Nicosia, Cyprus on May 22–23 for the informal ECOFIN and Eurogroup meetings hosted under the Cyprus Presidency of the Council. The agenda included discussion of stablecoins and digital assets financial stability risks, EU capital markets competitiveness in the context of the Draghi Report, and the impact of the Russia-Ukraine war and Middle East conflict on European economic resilience. ECB Governing Council members participated in a joint session with Finance Ministers — unusual at informal ECOFIN — reflecting the urgency of coordinating monetary and fiscal policy against an inflationary backdrop driven by energy price volatility. The Nicosia meeting also provided an opportunity for bilateral talks on the EU-US trade deal implementation timeline following the May 20 provisional agreement.

title: Hungary's Magyar Pushes Back on Pension and Tax Reforms as EU Commission Sends 20-Strong Team to Budapest
detail: Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar pushed back against European Commission demands for pension system and tax reform as preconditions for unfreezing approximately €17 billion in EU cohesion and Recovery and Resilience Facility funds, a Euronews report on May 22 revealed. A delegation of over 20 Commission experts arrived in Budapest for a week-long technical review of Hungary's compliance with 27 rule-of-law 'supermilestones', concluding May 22. A Commission official stated the delegation's size reflects 'von der Leyen's personal commitment' to the process. Despite Magyar's pushback on structural economic reforms, a breakthrough on Hungary's participation in the ERASMUS+ student exchange programme appeared within reach. Hungary faces an August 31, 2026 deadline to complete all supermilestones under its Recovery and Resilience Plan or risk losing its entire €10.4 billion allocation. Article 7 proceedings against Hungary — initiated in 2018 — remain formally open but are expected to be wound down as Magyar's government advances rule-of-law reforms.
